opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and honestly, my answer has changed a lot over the years.

When I was younger, I think my reward function was very sparse and very external: grades, publications, getting into the right program, getting the next title. Those are clean signals, easy to measure, but you only get them once in a while. And when you do get them, the satisfaction fades surprisingly fast. You optimize hard for something, you reach it, and a week later you're asking, "Okay, what's next?" That's a sign the reward is misspecified.

Today I'd define it as a combination of a few terms.

The first is **learning and understanding**: am I seeing the world a bit more clearly than I did yesterday? That could be a research problem finally clicking, or understanding a person better. It's an intrinsic reward, and it's dense. You can get a little of it every day, which makes the whole process enjoyable rather than just the outcome.

The second is **impact on other people**: did something I built, wrote, or said actually help someone? Not in an abstract, "change the world" sense, but concretely. A student who got unstuck, a colleague whose idea got better because we argued about it, a tool someone actually uses. I weight this heavily because it keeps me honest. It's easy to fool yourself about how smart your work is; it's harder to fool yourself about whether it helped anyone.

The third is **relationships**: family, friends, the people I trust. I used to treat this almost as a constraint, something to satisfy so I could get back to "the real work." Now I think it's a core term in the objective, not a regularizer.

And then there's a discount factor question. I try not to discount the future too heavily, so I'm willing to do hard, slow things that pay off over years. But I also try not to discount the present to zero. If you're always sacrificing now for some later reward, you can end up with a life that looks great on paper and feels empty.

So if I had to compress it into one line: maximize long-term growth and genuine usefulness, while actually enjoying the trajectory, not just the terminal state.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a loaded question to open with, because the honest answer is that I try not to have one.

Early on, I absolutely did. It was very legible: get into the right program, publish in the right venues, get the job that signals I'm good. And the thing about a legible reward function is that you optimize it extremely well and then wake up one day realizing you've been climbing a gradient someone else defined. You hit the local maximum and it doesn't feel like anything.

So what I do now is closer to a mixture. One component is curiosity, and I mean that literally: am I confused about something today, and did I make a dent in the confusion? That's a daily signal, and it's hard to fake. The second is whether the people I work with are better off for having worked with me. That one's slower, it's noisy, but it compounds. And the third is just honesty with myself about whether I'm doing the thing or performing the thing. Those look identical from the outside and feel completely different from the inside.

What I've dropped is the sparse, delayed stuff. Awards, recognition, the big milestone. Not because they're bad, but because if you make them the objective you're training yourself on a reward that arrives maybe once every few years, and you'll do strange things in between to chase it.

The uncomfortable part is that I still catch myself reward hacking. I'll notice I'm choosing a project because it'll look good rather than because I actually want to know the answer. I don't think you ever fully fix that. You just get a little faster at catching it.

I don’t want to optimize so hard for some future outcome that I miss the process of getting there.

sol-6.1.text: I think my reward function today is pretty simple: am I learning, am I doing something useful, and am I spending my time with people I care about? Those things don’t always line up perfectly. Something can be intellectually exciting but not particularly useful, or professionally rewarding but take too much away from the rest of life. So I try to look at the whole picture. If I’m growing, contributing, and enjoying the people I’m on the journey with, that feels like a good outcome.
